_comment: Innovation proposals — a concept a worker found worth cooking, not a bug fix. Nothing here is implemented from the proposal alone; it has to move through the status lifecycle. Never discard an entry for being 'not immediately useful' -- park it with a reason instead of deleting it.

entry_schema.hypothesis: the falsifiable claim, e.g. 'X currently fails at Y; with Z it succeeds' -- not 'would be cool'
entry_schema.originating_agent: model + task_key of the worker that proposed it
entry_schema.supporting_evidence: what grounds this in an actual observed failure mode -- a scenario-suite result, a ledger entry, a named pattern from comparable tools
entry_schema.estimated_upside: concrete and bounded, not a multiplier -- what measurably improves and by roughly how much, with the honesty that this is a pre-benchmark estimate
entry_schema.dependencies: what this needs to exist first
entry_schema.experiment_required: the specific benchmark or adversarial test that would confirm or kill it
entry_schema.status_reason: required whenever status is rejected or parked -- why, so it can be revisited if the reason stops applying

entries.hypothesis: A priority-ordered, character-budget-aware pruning pass over the DOM/AX snapshot (focused/invalid fields+alerts first, then actionable controls, then repeated records breadth-first, then named sections, then low-value text, with a recoverable omission marker) reduces per-step tokens without losing actionable elements, on pages currently producing oversized snapshots.
entries.originating_agent: orchestrator, from reading agentrhq/webcmd (competitive analysis, docs/agent-notes/competitive-analysis.md)
entries.supporting_evidence: webcmd cites this as one of three changes behind its BU Bench V1 token/accuracy numbers versus browser-use -- self-reported, not yet independently reproduced, but the technique itself is inspectable in their public writeup
entries.estimated_upside: unmeasured -- webcmd claims ~10% fewer tokens than browser-use in their run; ours would need its own measurement, not theirs
entries.implementation_cost: medium -- touches the DOM serialization path some existing tests already cover; needs its own scenario coverage before landing
entries.dependencies: the local failure-scenario suite (planned, not yet built) to have a real before/after to measure against
entries.experiment_required: reproduce BU Bench V1 (or a subset) against current browser-use to get OUR baseline numbers first, before building anything -- a prototype without that baseline cant be judged

entries.hypothesis: Returning a structural diff of page state after a browser-run program (instead of a fresh full snapshot), with an explicit opt-out for research-style tasks, reduces tokens on form-filling/multi-step workflows without losing the agent visibility into what changed.
entries.supporting_evidence: same source as above; webcmd explicitly reran both task categories to check the opt-out did not regress research-task accuracy before shipping it
entries.implementation_cost: medium-high -- needs a real diffing strategy against this repo own snapshot format, plus the same before/after discipline webcmd applied (rerun both task types, not just the one being optimized)
entries.dependencies: the failure-scenario suite; also depends on idea 1 if snapshot pruning changes the format being diffed
entries.experiment_required: a scenario/benchmark showing token reduction on multi-step form tasks with zero regression on research-style tasks

entries.hypothesis: Encouraging more aggressive batched code-based execution (multiple browser steps in one agent turn) measurably lowers agent-turns-per-task, the same lever webcmd attributes part of its turn-count advantage to.
entries.supporting_evidence: webcmd states this as one of three factors behind its 9.8-vs-14.8 turns/task number; this repo already has a code-execution-over-page action per its own project history, so the question is usage rate, not whether the capability exists
entries.estimated_upside: unmeasured -- needs a baseline read of how often the existing action is actually invoked vs single-step actions across a real task sample
entries.implementation_cost: low to start (measurement only), unknown for any follow-on change
entries.dependencies: none to start measuring; the failure-scenario suite for a controlled comparison
entries.experiment_required: first just measure: what fraction of current real task runs use the batched action vs single steps, before proposing any change to encourage it more

entries.hypothesis: Extending browser_use/synthesis (currently a per-origin tool manifest) to also record observed pitfalls and fallback paths, not just available actions, would close a gap against webcmds broader sitemap concept.
entries.supporting_evidence: webcmd README describes its sitemap layer as covering pages, states, actions, workflows, APIs, pitfalls, and fallback paths -- broader than a tool manifest; not yet compared against SiteToolSynthesizer/ManifestStore in detail
entries.estimated_upside: unmeasured -- this one needs a real side-by-side reading of both systems before its even clear how big the gap is
entries.implementation_cost: unknown -- parked pending the comparison, not sized yet
entries.dependencies: a focused read of both browser_use/synthesis/{service,store,views}.py and webcmds src/site-memory/ (concepts only, still no code copying)
entries.experiment_required: the comparison itself, before any implementation cost estimate is trustworthy
entries.status_reason: least concrete of the four -- needs a dedicated comparison pass before its even scoped, not ready for a prototype yet
